extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, museum professionals, and educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial-style discussion proposing standards and an inquiry into the organisation, purpose, and administration of museums in the United Kingdom, arguing for reforms, coordination, and professional staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum curator qualifications and remuneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Museum curators must be highly trained men and women of broad education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Museums Association urges that curators be highly trained and broadly educated; the only way to obtain such people is to offer an adequate salary. (Context: recommendation as part of reform proposals to professionalise museum staff.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Museums' core method and identity
rubrics_metrics.description: All museums work by the same method — the accumulation, preservation, and demonstration of concrete objects; they are guided by the same broad principles and need the same kind of assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any inquiry or reform should treat museums as museums (not confuse them with educational, industrial, or artistic institutions), and recognise their shared core functions when proposing standards or coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a museum inquiry — broad, museum-centred approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Any such inquiry should approach the subject on the broadest possible lines; the resolution asks for a report upon the work of the museums of the United Kingdom in relation to industries and general culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inquiry should deal with museums as such in relation to all their multifarious aims and activities (industrial, educational, artistic, etc.), seeking a harmonious collaboration rather than narrow compartmentalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of overlap, waste, and poor coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need to remedy the waste of material, waste of money, and waste of effort that are the consequences of overlapping, competition, lack of co-ordination, inappropriate administration, unequal distribution of funds, and other evils inherent in disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should aim to reduce duplication and competition between museums, improve administration and coordination, and address unequal funding distribution to make better collective use of resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museums' roles: industry, general culture, and education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Museums Association resolution requests a report on museums' work 'in relation to industries and general culture.' 'General culture' presumably includes scholastic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a museum's value, consider its contributions to industrial application, technical/artistic support, scholastic education, and broader cultural enrichment; industrial utility has been recognised by bodies such as the Federation of British Industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and economy of reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: A large amount of reform might be effected without material increase of expenditure; indeed, some of the obviously desirable reforms would tend to economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals for reorganisation should prioritise measures that can be implemented without large additional spending and that may produce cost savings or greater efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic-measurement methodological assumption (research example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocity constants were calculated, assuming the reaction to be expressible by a simple chemical equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving rate constants from spectroscopic perturbation experiments, it may be appropriate to assume a simple chemical equation for the reaction — but this is an explicit modelling assumption that should be stated and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation-measurement method for rapid reactions (research example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure reaction velocity by displacing equilibrium (here by light) and monitoring reversion with a spectroscope; two methods used: (a) flow from light-exposed tube into dark tube with spectroscopic sampling along flow; (b) sudden cutoff of light in a vessel and timing reversion with a chronometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perturbation (e.g., light) to displace equilibrium and high-time-resolution optical measurement to follow relaxation; select a measurement protocol (flow-through vs. sudden cutoff) appropriate to reaction timescale and experimental constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical weather-prediction formulation (modelling standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather prediction by numerical process should be based on seven fundamental formulae: three equations for time-rate of change of the easterly, northerly, and vertical components of momentum; three for density, water-content, and heat-content; and the gas equation for air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A numerical scheme should represent the essential dynamics and thermodynamics (momentum, mass, moisture, heat, equation of state) to capture atmospheric evolution; these form the minimal set of prognostic variables in Richardson's formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-difference lattice and resolution choices in NWP (modelling standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The atmosphere is represented by a lattice of representative points (a 'chequer') with squares 200 kilometres long, 3° of latitude broad, and 2 decibars of pressure thick; the standard time-interval over which uniformity is preserved is six hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select grid spacing and time-step appropriate to the phenomena modelled; Richardson suggests coarse slabs (~200 km, 3° latitude, 2 dbar) and 6-hour time intervals for his computations, and emphasises choosing representative points and sufficient vertical levels to characterise local weather changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling and vertical resolution in atmospheric modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The formulae all relate to an individual sample of air in a column at a single point; representative points are chosen for which changes are computed at a sufficient number of levels to give a working idea of changes in the weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discretising the atmosphere for numerical prediction, ensure that representative columns and multiple vertical levels are used so the model captures the vertical structure affecting weather evolution.
